nuggets.title: Cluster Rebalance Drops 15% of Keys During Scale-Out

scenario.symptoms: Adding nodes during peak causes GET misses and 404 spikes; clients hit wrong owners after ring change.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Consistent hash ring rebalances without virtual nodes; only minimal key migration protocol implemented.

incident.headline: Improper consistent hashing migration routes reads to wrong nodes

agenda.goal: Explain consistent hashing with virtual nodes to distribute data and enable scaling.
agenda.opener: How do you decide which node stores the data for a given key?

evidence.strong: Explains consistent hashing and virtual nodes, showing how adding a node only affects neighbours.
evidence.adequate: Mentions consistent hashing but struggles to explain how data rebalances when a node is added.
evidence.weak: Suggests modulo hashing, requiring a full cluster reshuffle on scaling.

misconceptions.pattern: Using key hash modulo N to find the node.
misconceptions.challenge: What happens to existing data when we add a new node to the cluster?

probes: How do we prevent hot spots if one node happens to get a much larger range of the hash space?
hints: What if each physical machine appeared on the ring in multiple different places?
agenda.referenceFix: The candidate used consistent hashing with virtual nodes for partitioning.

nuggets.title: Single Replica Loss Causes Durability Incident

scenario.symptoms: Disk failure on one node permanently loses writes that were acknowledged with W=1.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Replication factor is 3 but coordinator acknowledges after first local write without quorum.

incident.headline: Sub-quorum writes acknowledged before durable replication

agenda.goal: Describe replication factor, preference lists, and reading/writing to a quorum.
agenda.opener: How does the system ensure data survives if the node holding it goes down?

evidence.strong: Defines replication factor N, explains tunable R and W quorums, and calculates R+W>N for strong consistency.
evidence.adequate: Suggests replicating data to multiple nodes but does not articulate how reads and writes coordinate across them.
evidence.weak: Has the coordinator ack the write before replicating, risking data loss on failure.

misconceptions.pattern: Writing synchronously to all replicas before acknowledging.
misconceptions.challenge: If one replica has a failed disk and cannot write, does the entire put request fail?

probes: How many nodes need to acknowledge a write before we return success to the client?
What if we want to prioritize latency over consistency?
hints: Have you heard of the terms read quorum and write quorum?
agenda.referenceFix: The candidate defined a replication scheme using R and W quorums.

scenario.symptoms: Cart counters intermittently revert; two clients increment same key and one update vanishes.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Conflict resolution uses blind last-write-wins without vector clocks or merge functions.

incident.headline: Last-write-wins conflict policy drops concurrent counter updates

agenda.goal: Handle concurrent writes using vector clocks or timestamps and explain how conflicts are resolved.
agenda.opener: What happens if two clients write to the same key at exactly the same time?

evidence.strong: Proposes vector clocks to detect concurrent updates and passes both versions to the client to resolve.
evidence.adequate: Chooses last-writer-wins with timestamps, explicitly acknowledging that some data will be lost.
evidence.weak: Assumes a centralized lock or database will prevent conflicts, missing the distributed nature of the system.

misconceptions.pattern: Assuming physical timestamps across nodes are perfectly synchronized.
misconceptions.challenge: What if the clock on node A is running 50 milliseconds faster than node B?

probes: If we accept both writes to remain available, how do we merge them later?
hints: Instead of relying on timestamps, can we track the history of updates using version numbers per node?
agenda.referenceFix: The candidate addressed conflict resolution using vector clocks.

nuggets.title: Anti-Entropy Never Runs; Replica Divergence Grows

scenario.symptoms: Weekly consistency audit finds 0.3% key mismatch across replicas; manual rebuild required.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Read repair is off and background Merkle-tree anti-entropy jobs are disabled to save CPU.

incident.headline: Disabled repair paths allow silent long-term replica divergence

agenda.goal: Explain how nodes catch up after a failure using hinted handoff and anti-entropy.
agenda.opener: If a node is down for a few hours and then comes back up, how does it get the writes it missed?

evidence.strong: Combines hinted handoff for quick transient failure recovery with Merkle trees for background anti-entropy sync.
evidence.adequate: Suggests a background process to compare data but does not optimize how the comparison is done.
evidence.weak: Assumes the node just stays empty or relies entirely on read-repair.

misconceptions.pattern: Scanning and comparing all keys between two nodes to find differences.
misconceptions.challenge: If the nodes hold a terabyte of data each, how much network bandwidth will comparing all keys take?

probes: How can we quickly check if two nodes have exactly the same data without sending the data itself?
hints: Is there a data structure that hashes ranges of data into a tree to easily spot differences?
agenda.referenceFix: The candidate proposed Merkle trees and hinted handoff for replica repair.

nuggets.title: Gossip Failure Leaves Phantom Nodes in Ring

scenario.symptoms: New nodes never receive traffic; routing table still lists decommissioned hosts as alive.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Membership gossip stops after network partition; no centralized seed or failure detector cleanup.

incident.headline: Stale membership gossip routes requests to dead nodes

agenda.goal: Explain how nodes discover each other and detect failures using a gossip protocol.
agenda.opener: How does the cluster know which nodes are currently healthy and participating?

evidence.strong: Explains a decentralized gossip protocol where nodes exchange state and detect failures via missing heartbeats.
evidence.adequate: Mentions heartbeats but relies on a central coordinator to manage cluster state.
evidence.weak: Assumes static configuration where all nodes always know each other.

misconceptions.pattern: Using a single registry database for all node health checks.
misconceptions.challenge: If that single registry goes down, how do nodes know who is alive?

probes: How can nodes share this information without a central server?
hints: How does a rumor spread in a crowd without a central announcement?
agenda.referenceFix: The candidate explained cluster membership using a gossip protocol.
